newsitem.title: GERMANY: German minister wants EU-wide soya labelling.
newsitem.headline: German minister wants EU-wide soya labelling.

text.p: Agriculture Minister Jochen Borchert says Germany is unlikely to cultivate genetically altered food next year and will not go it alone on labelling such foodstuffs.
Borchert said in an interview with Focus magazine released ahead of publication on Monday that he wanted a European-wide solution on labelling genetically changed food.
"There are still some questions that have to be clarified at a European level," he said. "We have to inform people and for that we need sensible labelling."
He said a comprehensive and practical system for identifying the products must be found, to give consumers the option of using them or not.
"We hope the European Parliament will agree. The possibility of voluntary labelling (by firms) is already there," said Borchert.
Health anxieties about biotechnology are acute in Germany, where environmental group Greenpeace has gathered 120,000 signatures on a petition against modified soybeans.
Campaigners want crushers to segregate the beans and the food industry either to boycott them or at least to label products that might be derived from them.
Soya is used in some form or another in about 30,000 foodstuffs including margarine, chocolate and mayonnaise. Seed crushers say the beans are safe.
Dozens of genetically modified products are on the market already -- one is the "Flavr-Savr" tomato, genetically changed to slow the action of an enzyme that starts the rotting process.
The European Union has no full policy on genetically changed food, although it has approved the importation of some specific modifications.
On Thursday the European Parliament urged EU governments to segregate and specifically label modified soybeans.
Germany buys most of its soybeans in the United States, where a minute fraction of this year's crop has been produced from plants genetically altered to withstand a widely-used weedkiller.
